title: Family & work at speed
mission: Known ground — family, work, the clock — pushed to real listening speed. The family tree the way Palestinians actually draw it (عم is not خال), the working day with its شيكل-counting realism, and numbers that fly by until your ear learns to catch them.
sources: Forms cross-checked against Madrasa dictionary and Living Arabic Project (Levantine)
Urban Palestinian koine (Jerusalem/Ramallah); native-speaker review pending — low-confidence items avoided

lessons.title: Who's in the family?
lessons.canDo: I can follow someone walking me through their family — and never confuse the father's side with the mother's.

blocks.body: Arabic splits the family tree down the middle: عم is your father's brother, خال your mother's — Hebrew's one דוד covers both, so your ear has a new distinction to learn. Add سيدو and تيتا, the neighbors who count as family, and you can follow any family story.

cognate.note: Both from Greek ζεῦγος 'yoke, pair' via Aramaic. Hebrew kept the pair (בן זוג); Palestinian made the pair itself the husband.

example.en: My sister's husband works at the hospital.
His wife is from Nablus.

items.note: From امرأة. Possessed it grows a ت: مرتي، مرتو. Everyday and neutral in the dialect; the formal word is زوجة.

cognate.note: Proto-Semitic w- became y- in Hebrew: walad → yeled. Same root, same kid.

example.en: The kids are at school right now.

items.note: Singular ولد. Also 'boys' specifically, vs بنات — context decides.

cognate.note: أخ = אח, أخت = אחות — the whole sibling set is a freebie.

example.en: I have three brothers and two sisters.

cognate.note: Proto-Semitic ʕamm — the paternal clan. Arabic kept the clan's uncle (عم); Hebrew widened the clan into the whole people (עם).

example.en: My uncle Abu Samir lives next to us.

items.note: عمو is also how kids address any older man. عمة = paternal aunt.

example.en: My maternal uncle lives in Amman.

items.note: Hebrew has one דוד; Arabic files the family in two cabinets — عم/عمة father's side, خال/خالة mother's side. Mixing them up genuinely confuses people.

example.en: Grandpa tells stories about the old town.

items.note: Literally 'his master' — affectionate. The formal word is جدّ.

example.en: Grandma made maftoul for the whole family.

items.note: مفتول — Palestinian hand-rolled couscous. تيتا cooking it is half the culture.

cognate.note: j-w-r, 'to turn aside and dwell.' Arabic: the one dwelling beside you. Hebrew: the resident outsider — גר — who later became the convert.

example.en: Our neighbor Abu Elias is from Haifa.

items.note: You met جارتي in Umm Samir's rumor chain. الجار قبل الدار — 'the neighbor before the house' — is proverbial law.

cognate.note: q-r-b, near. Relatives are 'the near ones' in both languages — קרובי משפחה, قرايب.

example.en: Half the town is our relatives.

items.note: Singular قريب — which also just means 'near.'

blocks.title: Who's this in the photo?
blocks.situation: Salma shows her colleague Fadi a family wedding photo. Ten lines, the whole family tree — follow who's on which side.

lines.speaker: فادي
lines.ar: مين هاد بالصورة؟ عريس؟
lines.en: Who's this in the photo? A groom?

lines.speaker: سلمى
lines.ar: هاد أخوي الكبير يوم عرسه. وهاي مرته، رنا.
lines.en: That's my big brother on his wedding day. And this is his wife, Rana.

lines.speaker: فادي
lines.ar: الله يهنيهم. ومين الختيار اللي قاعد قدام؟
lines.en: Congratulations to them. And who's the old man sitting in front?

lines.speaker: سلمى
lines.ar: هاد سيدو، وجنبه تيتا.
lines.en: That's my grandpa, and next to him grandma.

lines.speaker: فادي
lines.ar: وهاد اللي واقف وراهم؟ شكله زعلان.
lines.en: And the one standing behind them? He looks upset.

lines.speaker: سلمى
lines.ar: ههه، هاد عمي أبو سمير. هو هيك دايمًا.
lines.en: Haha — that's my uncle Abu Samir, my father's brother. He's always like that.

lines.speaker: فادي
lines.ar: والمرة اللي حاملة البيبي؟
lines.en: And the woman holding the baby?

lines.speaker: سلمى
lines.ar: خالتي ريم، إخت إمي. والبيبي ابنها.
lines.en: My aunt Reem — my mother's sister. The baby is her son.

lines.speaker: فادي
lines.ar: عيلة كبيرة ما شاء الله. كلهم قرايب؟
lines.en: Big family, mashallah. All relatives?

lines.speaker: سلمى
lines.ar: قرايب وجيران — عنا الجيران زي العيلة.
lines.en: Relatives and neighbors — for us, neighbors are like family.

questions.prompt: Whose wedding is in the photo?
Who is sitting in front?
Abu Samir is Salma's…
questions.why: عمي أبو سمير — and عم is always the father's side.

questions.prompt: Aunt Reem is whose sister?
questions.why: خالتي ريم، إخت إمي — خالة is the mother's side, every time.

questions.prompt: What does Salma say about the neighbors?

items.en: That's my sister's husband — he works as an engineer.
My ʕamm is my father's brother.
My khāle is my mother's sister.

items.ar: ساكنين جنبنا من زمان — هم ____ منيحين.
items.en: They've lived next to us forever — they're good neighbors.
All the relatives came to the wedding.

points.explanation: Kinship words fuse straight onto possessive endings: أبوي my father, إمك your mother, أخوه his brother. The endings are the same ones from وينك — one quick syllable carries the whole relationship.

examples.en: My father and your father work together.

examples.ar: إمها من القدس وأبوها من الخليل.
examples.en: Her mother is from Jerusalem and her father from Hebron.

examples.ar: أخوه ساكن برة من عشر سنين.
examples.en: His brother has lived abroad for ten years.

points.explanation: Possessed spouses: جوزي، جوزها — and مرة grows a ت when owned: مرتي my wife, مرتو his wife. Hear the ت and you know a wife is being mentioned, not 'a time' (مرة also means 'once' — context and the ت decide).

examples.en: His wife is a doctor in Ramallah.
Her husband is away in the Gulf for work.

items.story: The oldest sound law you'll ever use: Proto-Semitic w- became y- in Hebrew. walad → yeled, and the same shift hides in dozens of pairs. When an Arabic word starts with و, try a י on it.
ʕamm meant the paternal clan. Arabic zoomed in — the clan's representative, your father's brother. Hebrew zoomed out — the clan of clans, the people. עם ישראל and عمي أبو سمير share a grandfather.

One root, j/g-w-r, 'to turn aside and dwell.' The Arabic جار dwells beside you and is owed protection; the Hebrew גר dwells among you and is owed protection — וְגֵר לֹא תוֹנֶה. Two legal traditions, one root, same ethic.
q-r-b — near. Your relatives are your near ones; so are theirs. Even the idiom matches: קרוב משפחה, قريبي.

lessons.title: What do you do for work?
lessons.canDo: I can follow someone describing their job, hours, and pay — including the complaint that comes with them.

blocks.body: شو بتشتغل؟ is the second question any Palestinian asks you (right after where you're from). This lesson is the working day: the professions, the دوام, the معاش — and the economics underneath, where an engineer's diploma meets a taxi's steering wheel.

example.en: I found a new job downtown.

items.note: The all-purpose word: شغل البيت housework, عنده شغل he's busy, شغلة a thing/matter.

example.en: I worked five years at the hospital.

items.note: Present بشتغل — you've been hearing it since Unit 1. Also 'to function': التلفون مش شغّال — the phone's not working.

example.en: My brother is a clerk at the municipality.

items.note: وظيفة = a position/job — the steady, salaried kind people pray for.

example.en: A math teacher in a government school.

items.note: Twin life: the classroom teacher — and the workshop boss or any respected guy: يا معلم! Note: מלמד looks parallel but it's root ל-מ-ד, not ע-ל-م — semantic twins, not cognates.

cognate.note: Hebrew borrowed the Arabic مهندس whole — same word, Hebrew vowels. One of the quiet Arabic loans inside modern Hebrew.

example.en: Her daughter is an engineer at a big company.

cognate.note: s-w-q means 'to drive (herds).' The שוק/سوق is where you drove them to sell; the سواق still drives. Market and driver, one root.

example.en: The serveece driver knows every road.

items.note: السرفيس — the shared taxi that runs fixed routes. Unit 3 rides it properly.

example.en: Work hours are eight to four.

items.note: School hours, office hours, your shift — all دوام. بعد الدوام = after work.

example.en: The salary comes in at the end of the month.

items.note: From عاش, to live — the living-money. Salaries 'come down' (بنزل) in Arabic. Formal twin: راتب.

cognate.note: b-ṭ-l, idle/void. Hebrew kept the idler (בטלן) and the void (בטל); Palestinian slid from 'idle' to plain 'bad' — الوضع بطال.

example.en: The economic situation is bad these days.

example.ar: ابنه خلّص جامعة وبعده عاطل عن الشغل.
example.en: His son finished university and is still unemployed.

items.note: A word doing heavy lifting in the West Bank and crushing work in Gaza. Street softer version: قاعد بلا شغل — sitting without work.

blocks.title: Abu Khalil, taxi driver
blocks.brief: One speaker, eight sentences, a whole economy. Listen twice before the transcript: how long has he been driving, and what's the story with his son?
preQuestions: How many years has he been driving a taxi?
Why won't his son come work with him?

transcript.speaker: أبو خليل
transcript.ar: أنا أبو خليل، سواق تاكسي من خمسطعش سنة.
transcript.en: I'm Abu Khalil — a taxi driver for fifteen years.

transcript.speaker: أبو خليل
transcript.ar: الدوام تبعي طويل: من ستة الصبح لتمانية المسا.
transcript.en: My shift is long: six in the morning to eight at night.

transcript.speaker: أبو خليل
transcript.ar: الشغل تعبان والبنزين غالي، بس الحمدلله.
transcript.en: The work is tiring and fuel is expensive — but thank God.

transcript.speaker: أبو خليل
transcript.ar: معاش ثابت ما في — كل يوم برزقه.
transcript.en: There's no fixed salary — each day brings its own.

transcript.speaker: أبو خليل
transcript.ar: مرتي معلمة في مدرسة بنات.
transcript.en: My wife is a teacher in a girls' school.

transcript.speaker: أبو خليل
transcript.ar: ابني الكبير مهندس — بس عاطل عن الشغل من سنة.
transcript.en: My eldest son is an engineer — but unemployed for a year.

transcript.speaker: أبو خليل
transcript.ar: بقوله: تعال اشتغل معي عالتاكسي. بضحك ويقول: يابا، درست خمس سنين!
transcript.en: I tell him: come work with me on the taxi. He laughs and says: Dad, I studied five years!

transcript.speaker: أبو خليل
transcript.ar: هيك الشغل في بلادنا — الشهادة في إيد، والإيد التانية فاضية.
transcript.en: That's work in our country — the diploma in one hand, and the other hand empty.

questions.prompt: How long has Abu Khalil been driving?
questions.why: خمسطعش — fifteen. The ـطعش ending is the teens' signature.

questions.prompt: His دوام runs…
What does his wife do?
His eldest son is…
questions.why: The diploma-in-hand line — the unit's whole economics in one sentence.

questions.prompt: «كل يوم برزقه» means…
options: No fixed pay — each day earns what it earns
He's paid daily a fixed wage
questions.why: رزق — sustenance, what a day provides. A worldview in three words.

items.en: I found a new job, thank God.
The salary comes in at the end of the month.
My sister is a teacher in a government school.
Things are bad these days — there's no work.
His son has been unemployed for two years.

blocks.title: Right now vs. always — and how long

points.explanation: بشتغل = I work (in general). عم بشتغل = I'm working right now. One tiny عم flips the timeline — and it's unstressed, so this is pure ear training. شو عم تعمل؟ asks what you're doing this minute.

examples.en: I've worked at the municipality for ages. (habit)
I'm working right now — I'll call you later.

examples.ar: شو عم تعمل؟ — عم بساعد أبوي.
examples.en: What are you doing? — I'm helping my dad.

points.explanation: Duration runs on صار + ل: صار لي خمسطعش سنة — it's been fifteen years for me. صار له سنة عاطل — he's been unemployed a year. Your Unit 1 صار, promoted to timekeeper.

examples.en: I've been in this job ten years.

examples.ar: صار لها شهرين بتدوّر على شغل.
examples.en: She's been looking for work for two months.

items.story: Modern Hebrew needed an engineer and simply took the Arabic مهندس (itself built on Persian andāza, 'measure'). Same word, retuned vowels — a loan hiding in plain sight in every Israeli office.
The root s-w-q means to drive herds. Drive them where? To market — the سوق/שוק. The سواق kept the original job: he still drives. Your shuk runs on a driving root.
b-ṭ-l: idle, void. The Hebrew בטלן idles; ביטול cancels into nothing; the Palestinian بطّال slid from idle to no-good. When work talk turns gloomy, this root carries it in both languages.

lessons.title: An ordinary day
lessons.canDo: I can follow someone narrating their day — start, finish, errand, collapse — verb by verb, at speed.

blocks.body: The day has a skeleton: بلش، خلص، رجع، وصل، نام. Hang a مشوار and an عزومة on it and you have Palestinian daily life. These are the highest-frequency verbs you'll ever learn — and the negation that wraps them, ما...ش, is this lesson's real boss.

example.ar: بصحى كل يوم خمسة ونص الصبح.
example.en: I wake up every day at five thirty in the morning.

items.note: You met بصحى in Umm Mohammad's routine. Synonym you'll also hear: فاق.

example.en: I started work early today.

items.note: The Levantine 'start' — MSA بدأ stays in the news. بلش الشتا — the rain has started.

cognate.note: ḥ-l-ṣ — to pull free. Arabic خلص: finished, free of it. Hebrew נחלץ: extricated. Done = out.

example.en: I finished my work and went home.

items.note: Bare خلص! is also 'enough! done!' — the conversation-ender you'll hear daily.

example.en: We came back from grandma's in the evening.

items.note: هلّق رجعت — you said this in Unit 1. Also 'again': رجع حكى نفس الإشي.

example.en: I arrived late because of the traffic.

items.note: وصلت وصلت! — 'I'm here, I'm here!' from Marwan at the roundabout.

example.en: I have a quick errand downtown.

items.note: Untranslatable gem: an errand, a spin, a short visit — any small going-out. Also a life's journey, in songs.

example.en: We're invited to dinner at the neighbors' on Friday.

items.note: From عزم, to resolve/invite. Careful with the ear: عَزومة is dinner, أَزمة is a traffic jam. One vowel between feast and gridlock.

example.en: It's been a long day — I'm tired.

items.note: Also 'in bad shape' generally: الوضع تعبان, السيارة تعبانة. Abu Khalil's الشغل تعبان.

cognate.note: n-w-m. Hebrew kept the doze — נמנם, תנומה; Arabic made it the whole night. אל ינום שומר ישראל uses your verb.

example.en: The kids went to sleep early yesterday.
My father is busy all week.

items.note: Same شغل root, passive shape: occupied. Also the phone: الخط مشغول — the line is busy.

blocks.title: Where were you all day?
blocks.situation: Abu Yousef comes home at seven in the evening — Umm Yousef has questions. (Yes, the electricity couple from Unit 1. He's hiding something about tomorrow's dinner.)

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.ar: وينك من الصبح؟ صحيت وما لقيتك.
lines.en: Where have you been since morning? I woke up and didn't find you.

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.ar: بلشت الدوام بكير اليوم — ستة ونص.
lines.en: I started work early today — six thirty.

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.ar: وليش راجع هلّق؟ الساعة سبعة المسا!
lines.en: And why are you back only now? It's seven in the evening!

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.ar: خلصت الشغل وكان عندي مشوار بالبلد.
lines.en: I finished work and had an errand downtown.

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.ar: مشوار شو؟
lines.en: What errand?

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.ar: جبت إشي لعزومة بكرا. مش رح أقولك شو.
lines.en: I got something for tomorrow's dinner. I'm not telling you what.

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.ar: يا زلمة احكي! شو جبت؟
lines.en: Come on, man, talk! What did you get?

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.ar: صبري عليّ. وين الولاد؟
lines.en: Be patient with me. Where are the kids?

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.ar: ناموا قبل شوي — كانوا تعبانين من المدرسة.
lines.en: They fell asleep a little while ago — tired from school.

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.ar: منيح. أنا كمان تعبان، بدي أنام بدري.
lines.en: Good. I'm tired too — I want to sleep early.

questions.prompt: When did Abu Yousef start work?
Why is he back so late?
What did he bring from downtown?
options: إشي للعزومة — ومش رح يقول شو
questions.why: مش رح أقولك شو — the رح future, negated. Tomorrow's dinner stays a secret.

questions.prompt: Why did the kids sleep early?
What does Abu Yousef want now?

items.en: I finished my work and went home.
I have a quick errand downtown.
The kids went to sleep early yesterday.
We're invited to dinner at the neighbors' on Friday.
I'm tired — I want to sleep.

points.explanation: Palestinian negation wraps the verb: ما in front, ش behind. In fast speech the ما often drops and the ش alone carries it: بشتغلش. Train your ear on that final ش — it's the difference between working Fridays and not.

examples.en: I don't work on Fridays.
I haven't finished the work yet.
I didn't sleep well yesterday.

points.explanation: لسا flips with polarity: before an adjective it's 'still' (لسا بكير — it's still early, from the pharmacy call); with a negative verb it's 'not yet' (لسا ما وصلوش). One word, both ends of waiting.

examples.en: They haven't arrived back from the errand yet.
Still tired from yesterday?

items.story: n-w-m: Hebrew kept the light doze — נמנם, תנומה, אל ינום — while Arabic stretched it across the whole night. When the kids ناموا, they did the thing the שומר ישראל famously doesn't.

ḥ-l-ṣ is pulling something free. Hebrew extricates — נחלץ מהבוץ; Arabic finishes — خلصت الشغل: I pulled free of it. And bare خلص! is the universal 'enough' — the act of pulling yourself out of a conversation.

lessons.title: Numbers & hours, by ear
lessons.canDo: I can catch numbers, ages, and clock times in real speech — including the backwards ones (عشرة إلا ربع).

blocks.body: Numbers are where listening actually fails: they fly past in half a syllable and carry the whole fact — the age, the price, the time, the count. This lesson is a number gym. The drills after the listening are the unit's hardest and most useful minutes.

example.en: It's quarter past eleven.

items.note: The teens all end in ـعش: اتنعش 12، تلتطعش 13، أربعطعش 14... hear that ending and you know you're in 11–19 territory.

example.en: I've been here fifteen years.

items.note: Abu Khalil's fifteen. The classic ear-trap pair: خمسطعش 15 vs خمسين 50 — the drills below hammer it.

cognate.note: ʕ-ś-r — ten and its multiples match across the languages: عشرة/עשר, عشرين/עשרים.

example.en: The bus comes every twenty minutes.

cognate.note: Hebrew counts שלוש, but Aramaic counted תלת — and Palestinian تلاتة sits with the Aramaic. The substrate under the dialect is the same one under the Gemara.

example.en: She's thirty years old.

items.note: Ear-trap with تلاتة وعشرين (23) vs تلاتة وتلاتين (33) — drilled below.

cognate.note: ḥ-m-š — five and fifty walk together in both languages: خمسة/חמש, خمسين/חמישים.

example.en: The trip costs fifty shekels.

items.note: Yes — شيكل. West Bank prices run in the currency you know, pronounced the Arabic way.

cognate.note: miyyeh is מאה with Palestinian vowels — same ancient hundred.

example.en: There are a hundred people at the dinner!

items.note: ميتين 200, تلاتمية 300 — the hundreds stack the same way.

example.en: It's half past four.

items.note: From نصف. Everywhere: نص ساعة half an hour, نص المعاش half the salary, نص الليل midnight.

cognate.note: r-b-ʕ — the quarter is identical: ربع ساعة = רבע שעה, sound for sound almost.

example.en: I'll arrive in a quarter of an hour.
It's a quarter to ten. (9:45)

items.note: Time runs backwards with إلا, exactly like רבע ל: عشرة إلا ربع = 9:45, not 10:15. The drills will test you on this — everyone falls for it once.

example.en: How old are you?

items.note: Answer: عمري + number + سنة. Bonus idiom: عمري ما... = never in my life — عمري ما سمعت هيك إشي.

blocks.title: Umm Fadi, in numbers
blocks.brief: A family portrait told entirely in numbers: ages, floor, clock, shift. Listen with a pencil — the after-questions are number-catching drills, and one of them involves إلا.
preQuestions: How old is her husband? (It goes by in half a second.)
What floor do they live on, and what's the house number?
Her shift starts with an إلا — what time is it really?

transcript.speaker: أم فادي
transcript.ar: بدي أحكيلكم عن عيلتي — بس بالأرقام.
transcript.en: Let me tell you about my family — but in numbers.

transcript.speaker: أم فادي
transcript.ar: جوزي عمره خمسة وأربعين سنة. وأنا؟ ما بقول.
transcript.en: My husband is forty-five. Me? I'm not saying.

transcript.speaker: أم فادي
transcript.ar: عنا أربع ولاد: الكبيرة عمرها اتنعش، والصغير عمره أربع سنين.
transcript.en: We have four kids: the eldest is twelve, the youngest is four.

transcript.speaker: أم فادي
transcript.ar: بيتنا رقم تلاتة وعشرين، الطابق التاني.
transcript.en: Our building is number twenty-three, second floor.

transcript.speaker: أم فادي
transcript.ar: بصحى الساعة خمسة ونص، وبنام إحدعش ونص.
transcript.en: I wake at five thirty and sleep at eleven thirty.

transcript.speaker: أم فادي
transcript.ar: الدوام تبعي من سبعة إلا ربع لتلاتة.
transcript.en: My shift runs from quarter to seven until three.

transcript.speaker: أم فادي
transcript.ar: جوزي بشتغل ستة أيام وبستريح يوم واحد.
transcript.en: My husband works six days and rests one.

transcript.speaker: أم فادي
transcript.ar: هاي حياتنا: كلها أرقام — والحمدلله على كل حال.
transcript.en: That's our life: all numbers — and thank God regardless.

questions.prompt: How old is her husband?
questions.why: خمسة وأربعين — five-and-forty. Arabic says the small digit first.

questions.prompt: The building number and floor:
Her shift starts at سبعة إلا ربع — that is…
questions.why: إلا subtracts: seven minus a quarter. The single most-missed listening detail in Levantine.

questions.prompt: When does she go to sleep?
questions.why: إحدعش ونص — the ـعش ending says teens… of the clock.

questions.prompt: Play it. Which number did you hear?
Play it. Which number did you hear?
questions.why: تلاتة وتلاتين — the doubled ت is your clue.

questions.prompt: Play it. Which number did you hear?
Play it. Which number did you hear?
questions.why: خمسين — the ـين ending = tens. طعش vs ين is the whole game.

questions.prompt: Play it. What time is it?
questions.why: إحدعش إلا ربع — eleven minus a quarter.

questions.prompt: Play it. What time is it?

items.en: I'll arrive in a quarter of an hour.
The bus comes every twenty minutes.

points.explanation: Palestinian time is arithmetic: ونص +30, وربع +15, وتلت +20 (a third of an hour — twenty minutes!), إلا ربع −15. The وتلت surprises everyone; the إلا ربع catches everyone. Both are constant in real speech.

examples.en: It's three twenty. (+a third)
It's six forty. (seven minus a third)
See you at quarter to eleven.

points.explanation: Ages: عمر + possessive, answer in سنة/سنين. And the idiom that makes عمر worth its card: عمري ما + verb = never in my life.

examples.ar: قديش عمر بنتك؟ — عمرها عشر سنين.
examples.en: How old is your daughter? — She's ten.
Never in my life have I heard such a story.

items.story: The Semitic hundred never changed hands: مية is מאה with the vowels relaxed. Same for the tens you already saw — עשרים/عشرين, חמישים/خمسين. Numbers are the most conservative words a language owns.
r-b-ʕ: ربع ساعة and רבע שעה are practically the same utterance. When a Palestinian says بعد ربع ساعة, your Hebrew ear already knows exactly how late they'll be.

Hebrew says שלוש — but its sibling Aramaic said תלת (תלת־ממדי survives in modern Hebrew!). Palestinian تلاتة keeps the Aramaic consonants. The dialect's deep layer and the Talmud's language are neighbors.

lessons.title: My people, my work
lessons.canDo: I can follow someone describing their obligations — who they visit, help, miss, and pay for — with the verbs' endings telling me who's who.

blocks.body: This lesson glues the unit together: family + work + the verbs of obligation between them. The grammar payoff is big — object endings (شفته، خبّرني، بساعدها) carry whole pronouns in a single sound, and رح opens the future.

example.en: This book is grandpa's.

items.note: The dialect's של. Kin fuse possessives directly (أبوي); things take تبع: الشغل تبعي، السيارة تبعتنا.

example.en: I have three brothers and a sister.

items.note: Arabic 'has' nothing — it puts things at you: عندي = יש לי, exactly the אצל logic. نمنا عند تيتا — we slept at grandma's.

example.en: I have to visit my uncle tomorrow.

items.note: Frozen form — no conjugation, ever: لازم أروح، لازم نروح. Negative: مش لازم.

example.en: Let me know if anything happens.

items.note: Your Unit 1 خبر turned into a verb: to news someone. خبّرني — the most common imperative in any Palestinian friendship.

cognate.note: š-ʔ-l: سؤال is שאלה. Even the kindness matches — سأل عن someone is לשאול בשלומו.

example.en: I asked about you yesterday.

items.note: سأل عن = asking after someone — care, not interrogation. اسأل عنّي — ask around about me.

cognate.note: z-w-r, 'to turn aside.' Arabic: turn aside to someone — visit (زار). Hebrew: the one turned aside — the stranger (זר). Visitor and stranger, one root apart.

example.en: We visited our relatives in Hebron.

cognate.note: š-w-q — longing. Genesis's תשוקתך and the Palestinian اشتقتلك share a root and an ache.

example.en: I missed you, grandma!

items.note: اشتقتلك — the ل fuses on: I-missed-to-you. The word every phone call home opens with.

example.en: I help my father with work every summer.

items.note: From ساعِد, the forearm — to lend an arm. الله يساعدك — the blessing for anyone mid-task.

example.en: I spend half the salary on the house.

items.note: صرف على = to provide for. The صرّاف gives out money — that's the ATM and the money-changer both.

example.en: Watch the kids in the street!

items.note: Literally 'turn your mind.' To a woman: ديري بالك. Farewell version: دير بالك على حالك — take care of yourself.

blocks.title: Samia's ledger
blocks.brief: A daughter, sister, employee, and neighbor counts her obligations. Every sentence has an object ending or a duty word — listen once for the story, again for the لازم/بساعدها/بخبره machinery.
preQuestions: How often must she visit her father?
Where does her little brother live, and how does she keep him in the loop?
What does she do for the elderly neighbor?

transcript.speaker: سامية
transcript.ar: عيلتي كبيرة — وكلهم بدهم إشي مني.
transcript.en: My family is big — and they all want something from me.

transcript.speaker: سامية
transcript.ar: أبوي كبير بالعمر، لازم أزوره كل يومين.
transcript.en: My father is getting old; I have to visit him every other day.

transcript.speaker: سامية
transcript.ar: وإمي بتسأل عني عالتلفون عشر مرات باليوم.
transcript.en: And my mother asks after me on the phone ten times a day.

transcript.speaker: سامية
transcript.ar: أخوي الصغير بدرس برة — بشتاق له كتير.
transcript.en: My little brother studies abroad — I miss him a lot.

transcript.speaker: سامية
transcript.ar: بخبره كل إشي بصير بالحارة، أول بأول.
transcript.en: I tell him everything that happens in the neighborhood, as it happens.

transcript.speaker: سامية
transcript.ar: الشغل تبعي منيح، بس بصرف نص المعاش على البيت.
transcript.en: My job is good — but I spend half the salary on the house.

transcript.speaker: سامية
transcript.ar: وجارتنا الختيارة، بساعدها بالمشاوير.
transcript.en: And our elderly neighbor — I help her with errands.

transcript.speaker: سامية
transcript.ar: هيك أنا: بنت، وأخت، وموظفة، وجارة. والحمدلله.
transcript.en: That's me: a daughter, a sister, an employee, and a neighbor. And thank God.

questions.prompt: Why must she visit her father every other day?
Who studies abroad?
questions.why: بدرس برة — and the اشتاق that follows is the unit's emotional center.

questions.prompt: What does she do for the neighbor?
How much of her salary goes to the house?
How many times a day does her mother call?
questions.why: عشر مرات باليوم — and بتسأل عني is the caring 'asks after me,' your سأل عن in action.

items.en: I have to help my mother at home.
I asked about you a lot — where have you been, man?
We visited our relatives over the holiday.
I missed you so much, brother.

points.explanation: Objects fuse onto the verb's tail: شفته I saw him, خبّرني he told me, بساعدها I help her, بزورهم I visit them. The pronoun is one unstressed sound — which is why untrained ears lose track of who did what to whom. Train here.

examples.en: I saw him yesterday at the market.
Tell me about the dinner early on.
I visit them every Friday after work.

points.explanation: The future is رح + bare verb: رح أزور I'll visit, رح نشوف we'll see. It's quick and breathy — sometimes just حـ: حنشوف. You met its negative in the dinner secret: مش رح أقولك.

examples.en: I'll visit grandpa tomorrow morning.
Who's going to help us with the dinner?

examples.ar: رح نخلص قريب، إن شاء الله.
examples.en: We'll finish soon, hopefully.

items.story: š-ʔ-l, to ask. שאלה and سؤال are the same noun; and both cultures ask after people, not just about facts — לשאול בשלומו is سأل عنه exactly.
š-w-q is longing. Hebrew gave it to desire — וְאֵלַיִךְ תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ — and Palestinian gave it to the phone call home: اشتقتلك. One root, both aches.

z-w-r, to turn aside. In Arabic you turn aside toward someone — a visit. In Hebrew the one who turned aside stayed outside — a stranger. The visitor and the stranger are one root apart; the difference is whether the door opens.

lessons.title: Review & free listening
lessons.canDo: I can follow real people telling family stories — how they met, who introduced them, how old they were — at street speed.

blocks.body: The family tree, the working day, the clock — now hear them braided together by strangers in Ramallah telling Corey how they met their spouses. جوز، مرة، قرايب، سنين — every answer runs on this unit's words. You will miss plenty; catch the skeleton.

questions.prompt: Play the word. What does it mean?
Play the word. What does it mean?
questions.why: خال = mother's brother. The axis question — forever.

questions.prompt: Play the word. What does it mean?
Play the word. What does it mean?
Play the word. What does it mean?
Play the word. What does it mean?
Play the word. What is the speaker doing?
Play the phrase. What is the speaker doing?

items.en: My sister's husband works at the hospital.

items.ar: عمي إخو أبوي، و____ إخو إمي.
items.en: My ʕamm is my father's brother, and my khāl is my mother's brother.
The shift runs from quarter to seven until three.
I've been in this job fifteen years.
I spend half the salary on the family.
He hasn't come back from work yet.

blocks.title: Real street: how did you meet your spouse?
blocks.titleAr: استماع حر — كيف تعرفت على جوزك؟
blocks.brief: The Ask Project again — Ramallah and around, one question: how did you meet your husband or wife? The answers run on exactly this unit's machinery: قرايب who introduced them, جامعة or شغل where they met, خطبنا (we got engaged), and ages and years flying by. Watch a few minutes; replay any answer that almost lands.
preQuestions: Family-arranged or chance? Count who says قرايب/عيلة introduced them vs who met بالجامعة أو بالشغل.
Listen for خطب/خطبنا — 'got engaged.' It marks the turn in almost every story.
Ages and years fly past: catch three numbers (عمري كان...، من عشر سنين...) and write them down.
